schools.summary: Gill would rather this verse closed the chapter before it, setting Esau and his posterity, who held their land as lords and proprietors, against Jacob and his seed, who held theirs as strangers; and he passes on the Targum of Jonathan's paraphrase that Jacob dwelt quietly, in tranquillity and safety, his brother being gone into another country. Calvin turns the same contrast into a lesson about faith: by Esau's departure the land was left to Jacob as its sole possessor, and yet in appearance he did not obtain a single clod of it, so that, contented with the bare sight of the country, he exercised his faith. He was no small gainer by his brother's removal, but the Lord willed the advantage to be hidden from his eyes, that he might depend entirely on the promise.

Henry marks the turn in the narrative: Moses has no more to say of the Edomites except as they cross Israel's path, and now applies himself closely to the story of Jacob's family, which is no bare barren genealogy like Esau's but a memorable and useful history. That Jacob is still a sojourner with a father yet living gives Henry his text, that we shall never be at home till we come to heaven. He then runs ahead into the verses following, with two observations that belong here because he makes them here: that Joseph, though his father's darling, was not bred in idleness, since those do not truly love their children who fail to inure them to business and labour; and that the father's love, however well founded in a dear mother lately dead and a grave and discreet child, was imprudently proclaimed by a finer coat, paternal government being obliged to impartiality.
Clarke keeps to the margin's rendering, the land of his father's sojournings, and places it probably in the vale of Hebron.

Ellicott says outright that this is not the beginning of a section but the end of the generations of Esau: we were told Esau went into a land away from his brother, then that he dwelt in Mount Seir, and now the necessary word about the other brother is added, the Hebrew using the same conjunction each time. Keil and Delitzsch explain instead why this generation begins where it does. The history of Isaac opened with the founding of his house at the birth of his sons, but Jacob was abroad when his sons were born and had not yet come into undisputed possession of his inheritance, so his own history starts with the return to his father's tent. Through this stretch the sons stand in the foreground, Joseph above all, who might be described as the moving principle of what follows, while Jacob remains the head of the house and the centre round which the whole revolves; and they divide the rest of his life at the removal to Egypt, noting that everything in the first part works toward the migration, directly by the sale of Joseph and indirectly by the alliance of Judah.

debates: Where the verse belongs. Gill would rather it closed the history of Esau, and Ellicott says outright that it ends the generations of Esau rather than opening a new section; Keil and Delitzsch treat it as the deliberate opening of Jacob's own toledoth, dated to his return to his father's tent.
themes: whether the verse closes the chapter before
the Targum's dwelt quietly
possessing Canaan by the bare sight of it
why the generations of Jacob begin here

schools.summary: Gill reports Aben Ezra and Ben Melech taking the word for events rather than descents, though he prefers to read it back to the chapter where Jacob's sons were listed, Esau's genealogy being a parenthesis after which the history resumes. Calvin makes it a record of events and not a pedigree, since Moses enumerates no sons or grandsons but sets out the cause of the brothers' envy. Of the evil report he reports the guess that some intolerable crime is meant, and prefers the reading that the boy complained of being vexed by his brothers' reproaches; he also asks a question nobody else raises, why only the handmaids' sons are named here, and suspects that sons of concubines would be quicker to envy, their servile descent exposing them to contempt. The love itself he thinks unremarkable, since aged fathers commonly favour a late child; what he finds monstrous is that a coat and similar trifles should inflame men to plan a killing.

Clarke takes the heading for the history of the lives and actions of Jacob and his sons, since nothing genealogical follows, though he allows the word may point back to the tables just given. On the word lad he chases the English instead, deriving it from the Hebrew for a child and lass from a contraction of ladess, and disposes of the story that King James had the word inserted, since it stands in Edmund Becke's Bible of 1549 and Coverdale's of 1535. Of the evil report he says the most useful thing in the chapter: conjecture has been busy about what it was, but the text is perfectly silent, and all we can make of it is that it increased a hatred first raised by the father's partiality and afterwards by the dreams. Wesley says only that this is no barren genealogy like Esau's but a memorable and useful one.

Ellicott alone reads the formula as a rule without exceptions: a man's generations are always the history of his descendants, as Adam's give the flood and Terah's the history of Abraham, so that this one runs to the end of the book. He renders the Hebrew as he was lad with the sons of Bilhah and takes it that the youngest had to wait on the rest, the sons being scattered in detachments across the country their cattle covered, and Joseph, brought up in Bilhah's tent after his mother died, naturally going with her sons. Keil and Delitzsch will not have the coat painted: it was a long coat with sleeves reaching to wrists and ankles, such as noblemen and kings' daughters wore, and not the coat of many colours Luther took from the Greek and Latin; the boy was loved above the rest as born in his father's old age, the first-fruits of the beloved Rachel, and that partiality is what made the brothers unable so much as to ask him how he did.

debates: What the formula means. Gill, Clarke, Calvin and Wesley read it loosely, as the history of events rather than a pedigree; Ellicott insists it is a rule without exceptions, a man's generations being always the history of his descendants.
outliers: Clarke's excursus on the English words lad and lass, and his dating of lad in Coverdale's Bible of 1535 to disprove the story that King James had it inserted.
themes: a heading that promises a genealogy
the lad with the sons of Bilhah
the evil report the text will not name
a long sleeved coat or a coat of colours

3.pericope_label: The coat and the hatred it raised

schools.summary: Gill grounds the preference in the boy himself, the firstborn of the beloved Rachel and a lovely youth, promising, prudent and pious; and he puts the brothers' perception of it to his words, his looks, his gestures, and above all the coat that marked him off from the rest.

Clarke renders the garment a coat made up of stripes of differently coloured cloth and finds his parallel in the toga praetexta of Roman youth, white and striped or fringed with purple, worn until seventeen and then exchanged for the plain toga virilis; such vestures of distinction, he adds, are worn all over Persia, India and China still. He will not let the partiality pass, since it is no wonder the brethren envied when the father had made the boy so distinguished an object of his love, and the old fable of the ape that hugged her favourite cub to death was directed against just such fondness. On their being unable to speak peaceably he corrects the English: it does not mean they were continually quarrelling, but that they would not give him the salam, the eastern greeting that comprehends every blessing and is therefore withheld from men one does not cordially wish well. Wesley says only that the coat was probably significant of farther honours intended him.

Ellicott takes the phrase son of his old age for a chronological difficulty, since Jacob was ninety-one when Joseph was born and older still at Benjamin's birth; the epithet becomes intelligible only if he waited twenty-seven years after his marriage with Rachel. He sets out both explanations of the coat, the long garment with sleeves and the patchwork of various colours, and prefers the second on the evidence of the tomb at Beni-Hassan, where captive Jebusites appear in rich robes whose patterns seem produced by sewing together small pieces of different colours. He will not follow those who take the dress for a formal designation of Joseph as head of the family in Reuben's room, since the point is doubtful and it was Judah to whom Jacob gave the right of primogeniture. Keil and Delitzsch add that the hatred was increased when the dreams came, the sheaves pointing to supremacy over the brethren and the sun, moon and stars to supremacy over the whole house of Israel, the repetition seeming to establish the thing as certain.

debates: What the coat was. Clarke makes it stripes of differently coloured cloth and Ellicott prefers patchwork on archaeological grounds, against the long sleeved garment Keil and Delitzsch insist on.
themes: kethoneth passim and the toga praetexta
the patchwork robes of Beni-Hassan
they would not give him the salam
the dreams that increased the hatred

schools.summary: Gill has him tell the dream in the simplicity of his heart, not understanding it or imagining there was any meaning in it, with no design to affront but as an amusement and for their diversion.

Henry accounts for the gift by the boy who received it: at about seventeen he was already pious and devout and well-inclined, which fitted him for God's gracious discoveries of himself, and because a great deal of trouble lay before him God gave him betimes this prospect of his advancement, as Christ had a joy set before him. He reads both dreams together and finds the second a wider emblem of the first, the empty sheaves bowing to the full one intimating the very occasion of the homage; yet Joseph was more of a prophet than a politician, or he would have kept the telling to himself. The observation Henry presses hardest is that Joseph dreamed of his preferment but did not dream of his imprisonment, as many young people setting out in the world think of nothing but prosperity. He finds a double irony in the sequel, that men who were enemies to the dream's accomplishment became its expositors, and that while they committed crimes to defeat it they were the instruments of accomplishing it; and he treats the father gently, as checking the boy to lessen the offence and, like Mary, keeping these things in his heart.

Wesley keeps the first half of Henry's account and lets the rest go: though very young, about seventeen years old, Joseph was pious and devout, and this fitted him for God's gracious discoveries; and since a great deal of trouble lay before him, God gave him betimes this prospect of his advancement, to support and comfort him.

Ellicott weighs the dream as revelation. Dreams as a rule do but arise from a mind wearied with overmuch business or from other trivial causes, yet God uses them from time to time for providential purposes, and they are then described as a lower kind of prophecy. In Joseph's life they form the turning point, and Ellicott notices that while revelations were frequently made to Jacob, no such direct communication from God to man is recorded until the time of Moses: the utmost granted to Joseph was to dream dreams, and after this the children of Israel in Egypt were left entirely to natural laws and influences.

themes: told in the simplicity of his heart
a lower kind of prophecy
no revelation recorded again until Moses
preferment dreamed, imprisonment not

6.pericope_label: The sheaves and the brothers’ answer

schools.summary: Gill prefers our version's modest hear, I pray you, to the reading of the Targums of Onkelos and Jonathan, hear now, and says plainly that the brothers understood the dream and its meaning better than Joseph did. Calvin ascends higher than the quarrel and reads the dream as election: Joseph had been chosen by the wonderful purpose of God for great things, and God revealed beforehand what he would do so that it might afterwards be known that nothing had happened fortuitously. It had been predicted to Abraham that his seed should be wanderers from Canaan, and this was the appointed method of the passage into Egypt, though from the facts first related nothing could have looked less likely. Two things he takes from it, that the Lord works by wonderful and unusual modes, and that he brings forth the salvation of his Church not from magnificent splendour but from death and the grave; and in Joseph, he says, a lively image of Christ is presented. He notices besides what the others pass over, that the emblem is a farming one though the sons were herdsmen with no harvest to gather, which he takes for a deliberate choice showing that the dominion rested on nothing they had at hand. The paternal favour of God, he ends, is like a fan to excite the enmity of the world, and the ill-disposed are often quick to perceive God's will and quicker to despise it, after which a stupor succeeds their quick-sightedness.

Clarke thinks the dream too plain to need comment unless the grain points forward to the plenty in Egypt and the scarcity in Canaan that drove the brethren down for corn, where it was fulfilled to the letter. Wesley gives the scorn in its own form, shalt thou that art but one reign over us that are many, thou that art the youngest over us that are elder, and finds in it the world's standing quarrel with the reign of Christ, our Joseph, whom an unbelieving world cannot endure to think should reign over them.
Ellicott makes stood upright the Hebrew for took its station, implying the position of chief, and infers from the emblem that Jacob practised tillage regularly, as was usual at Haran too.

themes: a celestial decree carried by circuitous windings
salvation brought out of death and the grave
a farming emblem given to herdsmen
the world's quarrel with the reign of Christ

schools.summary: Gill takes the second dream as relating to the same subject and given for the confirmation of it, the emblems only being different and more comprehensive. Calvin gives the reason for the change of emblem: the scope is the same, but to inspire greater confidence in the oracle God presents a figure from heaven, for the brethren had despised what was said about the sheaves and are now called to look upward, where his august Majesty shines forth. As for the objection that the mother was dead and could not bow down, he thinks the sense plain without subterfuges and the interpretation of certain Hebrews who refer the moon to Bilhah frigid: the sun and moon designate the head of the family on each side, so that Joseph sees himself reverenced by the whole house of his father.

Clarke pauses only to say that this dream is as clear as the preceding one, and then offers three ways with the difficulty about the mother. Perhaps Jacob, in the very form of his question, meant to hint at the impossibility of the dream's being fulfilled, one of the chief actors being already dead; or perhaps not, since any one wife or concubine was sufficient to fulfil that part; or Joseph may have dreamed before Rachel died, though even then she did not live to fulfil the part referring to herself. He then asks a question nobody else raises, why eleven stars, and wonders whether the Zodiac is alluded to, the eleven brethren answering to eleven of the celestial signs and Joseph to the twelfth, since the zodiacal constellations were distinguished among the eastern nations from time immemorial.
Ellicott makes the doubling a rule of this history: in Joseph's story the dreams are always double, though in the case of the chief butler and baker the interpretation was diverse.

outliers: Clarke's suggestion that the eleven stars allude to the Zodiac, Joseph answering to the twelfth sign.
themes: a figure fetched from heaven
who the moon could be
the eleven stars and the Zodiac
the dreams of this history always double

schools.summary: Gill says Joseph told it a second time in his brethren's hearing so that his father might pass judgment on it before them, and observes afterwards that all the father's precaution availed nothing, since they suspected the dreams portended Joseph's pre-eminence and envied him for it. Calvin will not let the rebuke stand unexamined. If Jacob suspected vain ambition he rightly reproved his son, but if he knew God was the dream's author he ought not to have expostulated, and that he knew it may be inferred from his afterwards considering the thing seriously, Moses distinguishing between the sons, who breathed nothing but the virus of envy, and the father, who pondered. It ought to have occurred to him that Joseph, though under his authority, sustained a prophetic character; Calvin's conjecture is that he feigned what he did not feel in order to appease contention, a method by no means approved by God. He should rather have said that if the dream were a common one it deserved ridicule and if it came from God it was wicked to speak against it. Of the sons Calvin notices the contradiction: they despise the dream, yet are not made angry about nothing, a secret sense of the Deity constraining them to feel there is something authentic in it while a blind ferocity impels them to a resistance against God they never intended.
Wesley reads the reproof as tactical, given probably to lessen the offence his brethren would take, though the father took notice of it more than he seemed to.

Ellicott thinks the rebuke deserved on its face, since in making the sun and moon bow down the dream seemed to violate the respect due to parents, and Jacob probably took his son's dreams for the fruit of a fancy dwelling on self-exaltation. On the persons meant he is blunt: Rachel was certainly dead, Joseph already having eleven brethren, and Leah never bowed before him either, for she died at Hebron. The enumeration of sun, moon and stars means Jacob, his wives and his children, the whole family, elders and juniors, a general phrase not to be interpreted too literally; though he allows that the handmaids, younger than either wife, may have gone down with Jacob into Egypt, and that Bilhah had probably done a mother's part by Joseph after Rachel's death.

themes: a rebuke that may have been feigned
a prophet under his father’s authority
sun, moon and stars as a general phrase
despising a dream they cannot dismiss

schools.summary: Gill allows it was usual to drive flocks far for pasturage, Shechem being some sixty miles from Hebron, but the marvel to him is the place itself: Jacob had bought a parcel of a field there, which gave them ground of their own to feed in, yet it was the town where they had destroyed all the males, and they might well have feared the neighbouring cities would rise and cut them off. Calvin reads the journey as an aggravation of what follows. Before treating the design of fratricide, Moses amplifies its atrocity by circumstances: the brother approaches in the discharge of a duty, comes by his father's command, obeys without reluctance, and though they had changed their place spares no trouble till he finds them. Their cruelty was therefore something more than madness, since they did not shrink from contriving the death of a brother so pious and humane; nor does Moses relate without a purpose that a man met him wandering and told him they had gone to Dothan, for the greater his diligence, the less excusable were they who repaid it so.

Henry draws the obedience out as a pattern: though the father's darling, Joseph was made and was willing to be his father's servant, and those best beloved by their parents should be the most obedient. He objected neither the distance nor the danger, though he knew they hated him, and that he did not turn home when he missed them at Shechem but sought diligently till he found them shows he travelled out of love and not in obedience only. What he met there Henry runs ahead to describe, fixing the moral on its deliberation: they conspired when they saw him afar off, not in a heat but from malice prepense and in cold blood, and the more of project and contrivance there is in a sin the worse it is, for it is bad to do evil but worse to devise it. In covering the deed with the tale of an evil beast they proved themselves worse than beasts, which do not prey on their own kind. Reuben, who of all of them had most reason to be jealous, proves the best friend, God being able to raise up friends for his people even among their enemies; and through it all God was overruling to make Joseph an instrument to save much people alive, in which Henry sees the type of the beloved Son sent out of his Father's bosom to his own, who consulted against him.

Ellicott answers the fear from the same episode: the sons seem to have retained Shechem by right of their high-handed proceedings, Simeon and Levi having added the households they seized to their own retainers until they could resist any attack of the natives. What strikes him instead is what the distance implies, a great idea of Jacob's wealth and power, that he should send part of his cattle sixty miles from home.

themes: feeding the flocks where they had killed
here am I
malice prepense and in cold blood
the wealth implied by sixty miles

schools.summary: Gill notices the courtesy of the wording, since the word rendered I pray thee may as well be rendered now, directly, immediately, which would agree better with a father's authority. On the stranger in the field he is cautious: many of the Jewish writers say this was an angel, and Gabriel at that, in the likeness of a man, and Aben Ezra makes him a traveller met on the road, but Gill prefers what Schimidt observes, that it was some man at work in the field who came upon him and took notice of him. He supposes too that Joseph must have described his brethren and said whose they were, or the man could not have known whom he meant.

Clarke reads the errand as a greeting: literally it is go and see the peace of thy brethren and the peace of the flock, which sends the reader back to what he had said about the eastern salutation the brothers would not give. He finds the reason for the father's anxiety in the old crime, the sons feeding on the parcel of ground bought from the Shechemites where they had made that horrible slaughter. He reckons the distances, Shechem about sixty English miles from the vale of Hebron and Dothan some eight miles beyond, and then withdraws his own confidence in them, warning that all such calculations are very dubious since we do not even know that the same place is intended, there being many proofs that different places went by the same names.

Ellicott adds the touch of character, that the sons were far too fierce themselves to fear any confederacy of the natives but Jacob was of a much more timid disposition. He locates the vale of Hebron by the pasture, the portion of Jacob's cattle that fed nearest home occupying the country immediately north of Hebron as far as the tower of Eder, and finishes the journey at Dothan, twelve miles north of Shechem in a small but fertile valley, famous as the place where Elisha struck the Syrian army with blindness. Not finding them, Joseph wandered about in the field, the open downs, until someone could inform him — whereas, Ellicott remarks, had he been a practised hunter like Esau he would have followed them by the tracks of the cattle.

outliers: Clarke's warning that the received distances are very dubious, since different places went by the same names.
themes: see the peace of thy brethren
a timid father and fierce sons
the tower of Eder and the vale of Hebron
a hunter would have read the tracks

schools.summary: Gill has them know him at that distance by his stature, his gesture or manner of walking, and above all by the coat of various colours; and following the Targum of Jonathan he puts the words into the mouths of Simeon and Levi, men so hot and bloody minded as the affair of Shechem showed, suspecting that this is why Joseph afterwards, as governor of Egypt, took Simeon and bound him. Calvin is severest here, and begins by praising Moses for the severity: so far from sparing his own family's fame, he brands its chiefs with a mark of eternal infamy, and profane history has nothing like nine brethren conspiring against an innocent youth. What is worse than the fury is the contempt of God underneath it, for they insult the youth only because a celestial oracle had called him to an unexpected dignity; and if they are indignant at the dreams, why do they not rather wage war with God? Not daring to assail him directly, they wrap themselves in clouds. The pretext is of a piece with it: it never enters their mind that what is hidden from men cannot escape the eyes of God, so stupid is hypocrisy, which flees the world's disgrace and is careless of the judgment above it. Turbulent envy drives them headlong to fight against God, who will always find a way through the most profound abyss to what he has decreed. Calvin closes on the comfort, that the promise which exalted Joseph almost plunges him into the grave, as those who have received the gratuitous adoption of God are permitted to be cast down until they seem nearer hell than heaven, and bids us fix his example in our minds that we be not disquieted when many crosses spring from the very root of God's favour.

Clarke renders their name for him lord or master of dreams, a form of speech conveying great contempt, and then passes the pit for indignation at the talk around it: what unprincipled savages, to speak so coolly of imbruing their hands in an innocent brother's blood, and how necessary a divine revelation is to show man what God hates and loves, ferocious cruelty being the chief characteristic of nations that do not receive the law at his mouth. Wesley marks only the coolness of it, that this was not in a heat or upon a sudden provocation but from malice propense and in cold blood.

Ellicott renders the phrase the same way, this lord of dreams, as expressive of contempt, and explains what they meant to throw him into: one of the pits, cisterns dug to catch and preserve the rain, dry in summer, deep and narrow at the top, so that a man cast in would have little chance of escape. He too reports that the Jewish interpreters accuse Simeon of being the prime mover in the plot.

themes: this lord of dreams
a crime with no parallel in profane history
cisterns dry in summer and narrow at the top
crosses springing from the root of God’s favour

schools.summary: Gill supposes Reuben overheard what was said without being in the consultation, perhaps because Simeon and Levi did not want the elder brother in the debate, knowing his temper more mild and gentle and fearing he would overrule them. Calvin thinks it worth observing by whose care Joseph was preserved while the rest were hastening to shed his blood. In one affair Reuben was the most wicked of them all, and that unbridled lust was the sign of a depraved nature; yet now he alone has regard to piety and, mindful of fraternal duty, dissolves the impious conspiracy. Whether he sought some compensation by which he might be restored to his father's favour Calvin leaves uncertain, but since Moses declares his intention was to restore the boy in safety, the conjecture is probable that he thought his brother's life a sufficient price. However that may be, the humanity he showed is proof that he was not abandoned to every kind of wickedness, and perhaps God by this testimony of penitence designed to lessen his former disgrace — whence we are taught that the characters of men are not to be estimated by a single act, however atrocious, so as to cause us to despair of their salvation.

Clarke grants that Reuben was a transgressor of no ordinary magnitude, if the earlier verse is taken according to the letter, yet his bosom was not the habitation of cruelty: he determined if possible to save his brother from death and deliver him safely to his father, with whose fondness for the boy he was sufficiently acquainted. He has no patience, though, with the embellishment of the scene, since Josephus in his usual way puts a long flourishing speech into Reuben's mouth which, being totally unfounded, is worthy of no regard. Wesley reads the proposal itself as the double thing it was, one his brothers thought would effectually destroy Joseph and one he designed should rescue him, probably hoping by it to recover his father's favour, which he had lately lost; and the whole of it, he adds, shows that God can raise up friends for his people even among their enemies.

outliers: Clarke's dismissal of the speech Josephus puts into Reuben's mouth as totally unfounded and worthy of no regard.
themes: the deliverer is the man who defiled his father’s couch
no character judged by a single act
a proposal meant two ways
Josephus and his flourishing speech

schools.summary: Gill reads Reuben's words against the original law: shed no blood, innocent blood, as the Targum of Jonathan has it, a brother's blood, the blood of one who had done nothing for which it should be shed, and which would bring vengeance on them. Calvin will not let the compromise pass for mercy. The pious fallacy he descended to proves how vehemently the rage of his brethren was burning, since he dared neither openly oppose nor dissuade them; nor does their consenting extenuate the cruelty, as though they were disposed to clemency, for better the boy should die at once by their hands than perish by slow hunger in the pit, the most cruel kind of punishment. Their gross hypocrisy is what should be noticed: they think themselves free from crime if only they do not stain their hands with blood, as if it made any difference whether they ran him through with a sword or suffocated him. When the Lord by Isaiah accuses the Jews of having hands full of blood, he does not mean they were assassins but calls them bloody because they did not spare their suffering brethren; and the sons of Jacob are nothing better, choosing a pit in the desert from which no mortal could hear his dying cry, though his sighing would ascend even to heaven.

Ellicott thinks Reuben pointed to some cistern in the desolate region girding the little valley of Dothan, and reminds us from a later chapter that Joseph begged hard for mercy and to be spared so painful a death, and that his brothers would not hear. He then turns from the pit to what the history has always been taken to mean: Joseph is nowhere in Scripture called a type of Christ, yet the Old Testament is so full of events which reappear in the Gospel narrative that the Fathers never hesitated to regard him so, the innocent delivered to death but raised thence to glory. He borrows Pascal's summary of the resemblances — the father's love, the errand to see after the peace of his brethren, the conspiracy, the sale for twenty pieces of silver, the rise from humiliation to be lord and saviour of those who had wronged him, and the two malefactors in prison against the two thieves at the cross. The history is also, he says, a vindication of God's providential dealings, every wrong being but a step in the pathway of Joseph's exaltation; and the descent into Egypt was an essential condition of the forming of the Jewish Church, since there alone could Israel have multiplied into a nation fit to be the depositaries of God's law. Keil and Delitzsch put the outcome in a sentence: Reuben had indeed saved Joseph's life by his proposal, but his intention of sending him back to his father was frustrated.

themes: shed no blood
a death by hunger is still a death
the Fathers’ typology and Pascal’s parallels
Egypt as the condition of Israel’s forming

23.pericope_label: Stripped and cast into the pit

schools.summary: Gill notes what came just before the violence, that Joseph had asked after their welfare in a kind and obliging manner and told them of the father's concern that sent him; and he identifies the pit as the very one Reuben had pointed to, whose counsel they gladly took and readily executed, supposing he meant the same thing they did. Calvin reports the guess that the coat belonged of right to the firstborn, so that Reuben was entitled to it until his misconduct forfeited it and Jacob transferred both it and the primogeniture to Rachel's eldest son — which, if true, would make Reuben's conduct here more generous than it appears; the objection is that Jacob is said to have made the coat for Joseph, not merely to have given it to him. What Calvin is certain of is that these men were full of fictions and lies, stripping their brother carelessly and feeling no dread at the pit because they hoped the crime would be concealed and his clothes carried home would raise no suspicion. Conscience is the fountain of modesty, but Satan so soothes those he has caught that the conscience which ought to have cited them before the bar of God only hardens them; and it is a reprobate sense that is withheld from a daring attempt only by fear of the shame of men.

Henry sees only spite in the stripping: each striving to seize the envied coat, they degraded him in imagination from the birthright, of which perhaps this was the badge, grieving him, affronting their father, and making themselves sport — now, Joseph, where is the fine coat? So, he adds, was our Lord Jesus stripped of his seamless coat, and so have his suffering saints been divested of their privileges and then made the off-scouring of all things. Of the pit he says they went about to starve him, throwing him into a dry one to perish with hunger and cold, so cruel were their tender mercies; where envy reigns pity is banished and humanity itself forgotten, and malice is so full of deadly poison that the more barbarous a thing is the more grateful it becomes. He fills in from the later chapter what this verse omits, that Joseph begged for his life in the anguish of his soul, pleading innocence, relation, affection and submission, and all in vain, Reuben alone relenting. Is this he, Henry asks, to whom his brethren must do homage? There he leaves the lesson: God's providences often seem to contradict his purposes at the very moment when they are serving them.
Clarke supposes a practical reason for taking the coat, so that if ever found he might not be discerned to be a person of distinction, and no inquiry made about him.

debates: Whether the coat carried the birthright. Henry supposes it was perhaps the badge of it, and Calvin reports the same guess only to note the objection that Jacob is said to have made the coat for Joseph rather than given it to him.
themes: where is the fine coat now
a dry pit and their tender mercies
the coat as a badge of the birthright
providences that seem to contradict purposes

schools.summary: Gill has them not at all concerned at what they had done, nor grieved for Joseph's affliction, but glad they had got him into their hands and were likely to be rid of him. Calvin calls it an astonishing barbarity that they could quietly feast while in intention guilty of a brother's death, since even the worst men are commonly afraid after a crime; and because the patriarchs fell into such insensibility, he bids us fear the same lethargy. In the caravan he sees the admirable progress of God's counsel: Joseph had already passed through a double death, and now, as if by a third, is beyond all expectation rescued from the grave, for what was it less than death to be sold as a slave to foreigners? His condition was made worse by the chance, since Reuben would secretly have drawn him out and brought him back; yet this was the secret turn by which God meant to raise him on high. Judah's speech has somewhat more reason in it, since he ingenuously confesses they would be guilty of homicide if they let him perish; and what Judah says of his brother, Calvin ends, the Lord by the prophet extends to the whole human race, so that whenever depraved lust impels to unjust violence we should remember the sacred bond binding society together.

Wesley reads the appetite as a verdict on the conscience: they felt no remorse, which if they had would have spoiled their stomach to their meat, and a great force put upon conscience commonly stupefies it, depriving it for the time of sense and speech. Clarke says every act here is perfectly in character, describing forcibly the brutish nature of their ruthless souls, and supposes a company of different tribes travelling together for safety, of which Ishmaelites and Midianites made the chief; the Chaldee calls them Arabians, from a root meaning to mingle, and the Jerusalem Targum Sarkin, what we term Saracens, while the Persian, he thinks, gives the true sense — a caravan of Ishmaelite Arabs came.

Ellicott traces the road: Dothan lay on the great caravan line by which the products of India and Western Asia reached Egypt, the route running north-westward round the Arabian desert, over the Euphrates, from Tadmor to Gilead, and over the Jordan at Beisan. On the shifting names he is firm — for Ishmeelites we have Midianites later and Medanites at the chapter's close, while the Targum and Syriac read Arabs, and probably these merchants descended from neither line by blood but belonged to some branch of the Canaanites, the great traders of antiquity whom Ishmael and Midian had subdued; the Jewish interpreters, reduced to great straits, even assert that Joseph was sold three times, whereas the three are one and the same, the names being borne only politically. The wares he identifies in turn: the spicery probably gum tragacanth, though some think storax; the balm the resin of the balsamodendron Gileadense, abundant in Gilead and much used for healing wounds; the myrrh certainly ladanum, gum of the cistus rose.

themes: eating bread beside the pit
a third death that was a deliverance
Ishmaelites, Midianites and Arabs
spicery, balm and myrrh identified

schools.summary: Gill makes the proposal opportunistic and dates it to the moment the caravan came into view: it was in sight of the Ishmaelites that the thought came into Judah's mind to get Joseph sold to them.

Wesley puts the arithmetic of it plainly — what profit is it if we slay our brother? it will be less guilt and more gain to sell him — and they all agreed to it. From the price he takes the comparison the whole tradition has taken, that as Joseph was sold by the contrivance of Judah for twenty pieces of silver, so was our Lord Jesus for thirty, and by one of the same name too, Judas. Of Reuben he supposes a kind project, that he had gone away intending to come round some other way to the pit and help Joseph out of it; but had it taken effect, what had become of God's purpose concerning his preferment in Egypt? There are many devices of the enemies of God's people to destroy them and of their friends to help them, and both are perhaps disappointed, as these were; but the counsel of the Lord, that shall stand. The irony Wesley leaves the reader with is that Reuben had it exactly backwards, since it proved that they would all have been undone if Joseph had not been sold.

Keil and Delitzsch read the absence from the brothers' side, and less charitably: the business was settled while Reuben was away, probably because they suspected that he intended a rescue. They call the rending of his clothes a sign of intense grief on the part of the natural man, and paraphrase his cry as a question about the reckoning — the boy is no more, and how shall I account to his father for his disappearance? The brothers were at no loss for an answer of their own, dipping the coat in the blood of a goat.

themes: less guilt and more gain
twenty pieces against thirty
the counsel of the Lord shall stand
the one brother not consulted

schools.summary: Gill gives the motive of the sale in one line — sell him for a slave, and that will defeat his dream — since the merchants were going down to Egypt and there would be no probability of his ever being lord over them; and on the two names he sees no problem, taking Midianites and Ishmaelites for near neighbours who joined in merchandise and travelled together, called Arabians by the Targums and by Josephus, which signifies a mixed people. Calvin cannot dismiss it so easily, since Midian was Abraham's son by Keturah and his sons therefore distinct from Ishmael's, and Moses has not put down the different names thoughtlessly. Some, he reports, think Joseph was twice sold in the same place; it might be better explained by supposing the caravan made up of both, the Ishmaelites giving their name to the whole while the Midianitish merchants were the actual purchasers; but Calvin's own reading is that Joseph was exposed for sale to any who chose, and the purchase being declined by the Midianites, he was sold to the Ishmaelites. The buyers might justly have suspected the sellers of theft, but the desire of gain prevented inquiry. From the merchants he draws a lesson about the two seeds: from Abraham's sons after the flesh a posterity so great was propagated that from both proceeded traders in various places, while the part of his seed the Lord had chosen was still small, for the children of this world, like premature fruit, quickly reach the summit of happiness, whereas the Church, slowly creeping through the greatest difficulties, scarcely attains in a long time to the condition of mediocrity.

Clarke thinks this the first instance on record of selling a man for a slave, though the practice doubtless began long before; the Anglo-Saxon renders it thirty pence, and where our translators supply pieces the Persian has miskal, probably intended for a shekel, which at three shillings each would make about three pounds sterling. He sets a modern figure beside it, having known a whole cargo of slaves, eight hundred and thirteen of them, bought by a slave captain in Bonny river in Africa at an average of six pounds each and paid for in guns, gunpowder and trinkets; and since only nine of the brethren were present, he works out that each had more than two shekels as his share in this most infamous transaction.

Ellicott measures the sum against the law instead: twenty shekels is reckoned in Leviticus the average worth of a male slave under twenty, about two pounds ten shillings of our money, though silver was of far greater value then than it is now.

debates: Who bought him. Gill takes Midianites and Ishmaelites for one mixed people; Calvin, holding the lines distinct, reports the guess that Joseph was sold twice and prefers that the Midianites declined the purchase and the Ishmaelites made it.
themes: sell him and the dream is defeated
whether Midianites and Ishmaelites are one
the price of a slave under twenty
the Church creeping while the world prospers

schools.summary: Gill supposes Reuben had pretended to go somewhere on business, meaning to take a circuit and come to the pit and deliver his brother and go home with him to his father, and reports the Jewish account that he departed and sat down on a certain mountain so as to descend in the night, as Josephus too makes it night when he came to the pit, calling to Joseph and, getting no answer, suspecting that he had been killed. On his return Gill has him suspect that the others had taken and killed him after their first design, since he had not been with them when they proposed the sale. Calvin reads the whole manoeuvre as a secret kindness overtaken by events: Reuben stole away under pretence of some other business so that, unknown to them all, he might restore his brother to his father, and there is no wonder he was anticipated when he had taken a course in a different direction, intending to reach the pit by a circuitous path. Only now, having lost all hope, does he unfold the intention he had not dared confess before, lest the boy should be immediately murdered.

Clarke observes only that Reuben was absent when the caravan passed by, to whom the others had sold him; and of the cry that follows he will not attempt a translation, saying merely that the words in the original are very plaintive.

Ellicott thinks the absence has been made into a difficulty when it really confirms the truth of the narrative. The difficulty arises solely from supposing that the brothers sat down to eat bread immediately after casting Joseph into the pit, an act well described as most cold-blooded; but the narrative says they were having their evening meal when the caravan came in sight, and between the casting in and the meal Reuben had apparently gone a long round to fetch in the more distant cattle, remaining away as long as possible so as to reach the cistern alone and send Joseph home before the rest could interfere. Keil and Delitzsch add the one fact none of the brothers knew, that while the father was mourning Joseph was being sold by the Midianites to Potiphar.

outliers: Ellicott's argument that Reuben's absence, far from being an inconsistency, fixes the meal as the evening meal and vindicates the chronology of the account.
themes: a circuit meant to end at the pit
the words in the original are very plaintive
an absence that confirms the narrative
sold to Potiphar while the father mourned

schools.summary: Gill draws two things from the taking of the coat: that Reuben, told what they had done and willing to make the best of it, joined the scheme; and that, since they had the coat to dip, when they drew Joseph out of the pit they did not put it on him but sold him naked. Calvin thinks the coat was carried by servants not accessory to the crime, since the sons and daughters are said soon afterwards to have come and consoled their father. Of the brothers he says that whatever they intended, their wickedness drove them to inflict a deadly wound on their father's mind, all the profit hypocrites gain by their disguises being that, wishing to escape one fault, they add sin to sin. But he will not spare Jacob either. It is a wonder that a man tried in so many ways, and always coming forth a conqueror, should now sink under grief — absurd that his son's death should cost him greater sorrow than the pollution of his wife, the slaughter of the Shechemites and the defilement of his daughter. Where was the strength by which he had prevailed even over the angel? The disposition to mourn teaches us that no one is endued with such heroic virtue as to be exempt from that infirmity of the flesh which betrays itself even in little things, whence men long accustomed to the cross, who like veterans ought bravely to bear up against every attack, fall like young recruits in a slight skirmish.

Henry gives the deception two purposes. The first was to clear themselves, for we have all learned of Adam to cover our transgression, and when the devil has taught men one sin he teaches them to conceal it with another, theft and murder with lying and perjury, though he that covers his sin shall not prosper long. The second was to grieve their father, contrived to be revenged on him for his distinguishing love: they sent the coat of many colours with one colour more than it had had, a bloody colour, and Jacob must be scornfully asked whether this were his son's coat, so that the badge of his honour became the discovery of his fate. Love is always apt to fear the worst concerning the person beloved, Henry says, and he asks those who know a parent's heart to put their souls into his soul's stead: sleeping or waking Jacob sees the beast setting upon Joseph and hears his piteous shrieks, and it added no little to the grief that he had sent the boy alone, so that he looks on himself as accessory to his death. The comforters Henry treats with contempt, since they might have comforted him by telling the truth; and he warns that we often perplex ourselves with imaginary troubles, when sometimes there needs no more to comfort us than to undeceive us.

Ellicott corrects the picture of the animal — the Hebrew is a full grown he-goat, not a kid — and passes on Maimonides' conjecture that he-goats were so often used for sin-offerings under the law in order to remind Israel of this great sin of their patriarchs.

outliers: Maimonides' conjecture, reported by Ellicott, that the he-goat of the Levitical sin-offering was meant to recall this crime of the patriarchs.
themes: one colour more than it had had
covering one sin with another
a veteran falling like a recruit
why he-goats served for sin-offerings

32.pericope_label: The bloody coat brought to Jacob

schools.summary: Gill has the coat sent by the hand of a messenger: the Targum of Jonathan names the sons of Zilpah and Bilhah, but more probably some of their servants, whom the brothers instructed what to say, not caring to appear in person at first lest the commotion they would be thrown into at their father's distress should lead on to a discovery. On the recognition he asks the reader to hear the verse rather than parse it — read without the supplement, the pathos appears the greater, my son's coat! — and to think with what a beating heart, what trembling limbs, what wringing of hands and faltering speech Jacob spoke it; the rending that follows was expressive of his grief for a son he supposed dead.

Clarke needs only one sentence for the manoeuvre — what deliberate cruelty, to torture the feelings of their aged father and thus harrow up his soul — and then supplies what made the father's inference so quick: it is likely he judged from the lacerated state of the garment, which the brothers, the better to cover their wickedness, had not only besmeared with the goat's blood but probably reduced to tatters. As this coat is rent, so is the body of my beloved son rent in pieces.

Ellicott reads the Hebrew as they caused it to go, that is, sent it by the hand of a messenger, and gives the same reason, that they were unwilling to see the first burst of their father's agony; the words that follow, he notes, were what the messenger was charged to say. Of the mourning he measures the length: Jacob mourned not merely during the usual period but so long as to move even the hearts of those who had wronged him, and probably he had several daughters by Leah and by the two handmaidens, Dinah alone being mentioned by name because two of her brothers forfeited the birthright by the cruelty with which they avenged her wrong.

themes: sent by a messenger, not by the brothers
my son’s coat
a coat probably reduced to tatters
the unnamed daughters of Jacob

schools.summary: Gill will not settle who the comforters were. His sons acted a most hypocritical part; as for his daughters, Jacob had but one that we read of, and the Targum of Jonathan makes them his sons' wives, though it is a question whether any of the sons were yet married, the eldest being not more than twenty-four, while the Jews hold that a twin daughter was born with each of his sons. Calvin measures the burden of the grief by the gathering: that they rose up implies a common deliberation, and hence appears how vast is the innate dissimulation of men, for the sons assume a character by no means suitable to them and perform an office of piety from which their minds are alien. Jacob's own part he handles more carefully than the words allow: to indulge grief knowingly and voluntarily is as good as rebelling against God, but Calvin takes the refusal to be limited to the alleviation men could offer, nothing being more unreasonable than that a holy man who had borne the yoke of God all his life should now, like an unbroken horse, bite his bridle. He thinks Jacob chides his sons angrily besides, as if to upbraid them by declaring that he esteemed this one son above all the rest. The excess itself he will not excuse, since a man so overwhelmed speaks of the grave as if the sons of God did not pass through death to a better life, and hence we learn the blindness of immoderate grief; the principal mitigation of sorrow is the consolation of the future life. Yet Moses' design, on his reading, was not to condemn the father but to set a mark of infamy on the iron hardness reigning in his sons, who saw him already dying through their wickedness and would not drop one word in mitigation of his sorrow when it was in their power.

Clarke allows the sons' wives may be included among the daughters, then turns on them: what hypocrisy to comfort him for the death of a son they knew was alive, and what cruelty to torture their aged father when there was no ground for it. Wesley reads the refusal as a resolution to go down to the grave mourning, and adds the maxim that great affection to any creature does but prepare us for the greater affliction when it is removed or embittered, inordinate love commonly ending in immoderate grief.

Ellicott takes up the word Jacob used for his destination, Sheol, which like the Greek Hades means the place of departed spirits, and notes that on his own supposition it can hardly be the tomb: believing Joseph devoured and unburied, he could not go down into the grave unto his son.

themes: who Jacob’s daughters were
an office of piety from alien minds
Sheol and not the tomb
inordinate love and immoderate grief

schools.summary: Gill distinguishes here what he had merged before: these were Medanites, sprung from Medan, a brother of Midian, distinct from the Midianites though dwelling near them and now in company with them and the Ishmaelites, all concerned in the sale. Of Potiphar he says the word for officer is sometimes used for a eunuch but cannot mean one here, since Potiphar had a wife and, some say, a child; and the title captain of the guard he takes of cooks and butchers, of whom Potiphar was chief, or rather of executioners, having charge of prisoners and of putting them to death, like our sheriffs. Calvin dismisses the first question — he is called a eunuch not because he was one, but because among the Orientals it was usual to denote the satraps and princes of the court by that name — and, tracing the second word from butchers to sacrificers to executioners, prefers prefect of the soldiers, not commander of the whole army but holding the royal troops under his hand, an office his own day would have to join with that of prefect of the prison. He calls it a sad spectacle that Joseph should be driven from one hand to another, no small indignity added to his former suffering that he was set to sale as a slave; yet the Lord did not cease to care for him, suffering the transfers so that it might at length appear he had come by celestial guidance to the dominion promised him in his dreams.

Clarke alone takes the literal sense of eunuch and defends it: lest it seem absurd that a eunuch should have a wife, he observes that in the east it is not uncommon, some keeping a whole seraglio though they appear to have no progeny, and discontent on that ground may have done as much for the unfaithfulness of Potiphar's wife as the motive commonly assigned her. He calls chief of the butchers a most appropriate name for the guards of an eastern despot, since if a man offend such a prince the order to a life-guard is, go and bring me his head, obeyed at once, without judge, jury or law. He ends the chapter with three observations: that the history beginning here shows such wonders wrought by Divine Providence as cannot fail to confirm our faith; that Joseph has often been considered a type of Christ, though where the Spirit of God has not marked a direct resemblance it is bold, if not dangerous, to call a man such a type; and that envy, which he defines as pain felt and malignity conceived at the sight of excellence or happiness in another man, ruins families, since a house divided against itself cannot stand and parents should take heed that their own conduct be not the first cause of it.

Ellicott reads the Hebrew as Medanites too, and gives three chief interpretations of the buyer's name: two Coptic words meaning father of the king, a title equivalent to vizier; Gesenius's reading of it as the same name as Potipherah, consecrated to Ra the sun-god; and Canon Cook's father of the palace. On the officer he offers two ways out, that the word had come to mean any palace officer or that Potiphar was chief of the eunuchs and so numbered among them; and on the title he sets the versions against each other, the Septuagint understanding slaughterers of animals for food and translating chief cook, the others the commander of the body-guard, which the same title borne by Nebuzar-adan settles.

debates: Whether Potiphar was literally a eunuch. Clarke alone defends the literal sense and explains the wife by it; Gill, Calvin and Ellicott all read the word as a title of court office.
themes: Medanites, Midianites and Ishmaelites
what the name Potiphar means
chief cook or captain of executioners
a caution against making types of Christ
